design_detail: Prospective single-group observational study (a case series without a comparison group) of urinary THCCOOH excretion in 60 adults who reported regular cannabis smoking and lived on the closed residential research unit of the US National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) Intramural Research Program under 24-hour medical surveillance with random drug tests, for up to 30 days of abstinence (observation 0.6 to 30.4 days per person). Every urine void was collected; specimens were screened by an immunoassay that is not named, at three laboratories, with 50 ng/mL or more counted as positive, and THCCOOH was quantified by GC-MS after alkaline hydrolysis (limit of quantification 2.5 ng/mL) and normalized to urine creatinine (ng/mg). Participants were grouped by the creatinine-normalized THCCOOH of their first specimen (0-50, 51-150 and above 150 ng/mg); times to the first negative and the last positive screen, specimens and peak concentrations between them and daily detection rates are reported by group, with each participant's values in Table II. Associations with baseline variables were tested by stepwise regression and by straight lines fitted through the three group means. Days since last use before admission were recorded (an independent variable in the regression) but are not reported, so every time in the paper runs from admission to the unit, not from last use. Filed as a case series and appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist for its descriptive estimates, as the round brief directs for case series.
can_establish: How long the urine of these 60 people, kept abstinent under 24-hour surveillance, went on screening positive for cannabis at the 50 ng/mL immunoassay cutoff after they entered the unit (in some, to the end of observation at about 30 days), and that the last positive screen came later in those whose first specimen held more THCCOOH per milligram of creatinine.
cannot_establish: How long after last use a test stays positive (days since last use are not reported); how long detection lasts beyond the end of observation (22 of the 54 participants who ever screened positive were still positive on their last day, 13 of 20 in the highest group); detection windows at other cutoffs or with other assays; or how well one person's first-specimen concentration predicts that person's window (the reported fits use three group means).

sample.recruitment: Healthy adults aged 18-45 who reported cannabis dependence or abuse (DSM-IV terms as used by the study) and had a positive urine cannabinoid test at 50 ng/mL were invited to live on the secure clinical research unit of the NIDA Intramural Research Program and were paid for time and inconvenience (p. 563, Subjects). How they were recruited, how many were screened and the dates of the study are not stated.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Inclusion: age 18-45; self-reported cannabis dependence or abuse; positive cannabinoid screen at 50 ng/mL supporting cannabis exposure; medical (physical examination, ECG, blood and urine chemistry) and psychological evaluation including drug-use history; normal serum creatinine (0.6-1.2 mg/dL) and no history or symptoms of kidney disease (p. 563, Subjects). No other exclusions are listed.
sample.demographics: 46 men and 14 women; 50 African American, 5 white, 3 Hispanic, 1 of mixed race and 1 American Indian; mean age 26.9 years (SD 6.4). By self-report: mean 9.4 joints a week (SD 9.7) on 10.6 of the last 14 days (SD 4.3), first use at 15.6 years (SD 3.2), 11.2 years of use (SD 6.4) (p. 563, Results 1st paragraph; Table I, pp. 564-565). Mean weight 170.6 lb, height 68.8 in; BMI per person is not printed.
sample.attrition: Not reported as attrition, but the length of observation ranged from 0.6 to 30.4 days (Table II, pp. 565-566) and reasons for leaving before 30 days are not given. 16 of 60 were observed for 27 days or more (editors' count from Table II).
sample.selection_effects: A paid sample from one research programme, 77% men and 83% African American, selected for reported dependence or abuse. Self-reported recent use ranged from none to daily: one participant reported 0 joints a week and no use in the last 14 days, another no use in the last 14 days, and 28 of the 57 with data reported use on all 14 days (editors' count from Table I), so the description as daily-to-weekly smokers (p. 563) does not fit everyone. Six participants (10%) never screened positive on the unit, so they arrived after their urine had already fallen below the cutoff.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported cannabis use (joints a week, days used of the last 14, age at first use, years of use; Table I) and the creatinine-normalized THCCOOH concentration of the first specimen on admission, used to form the three groups (p. 563, Statistics). Days since last use were recorded but are not reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Smoked cannabis; self-reported mean 9.4 joints a week (range 0-60) on 10.6 of the last 14 days, 11.2 years of use (Table I). The THC content and amounts of what was smoked are unknown.
exposure.polysubstance: Random urine tests for amphetamines, cannabinoids, cocaine, opiates and phencyclidine on the unit (p. 563, Subjects); use of other drugs, alcohol and tobacco before admission is not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Abstinence enforced by residence on a closed unit with 24-hour medical surveillance and random drug tests (p. 563, Subjects). Time since last use before admission is not reported.

comparison.controls: None. Comparisons are between three groups formed by the THCCOOH/creatinine of the first specimen, and associations with baseline variables within the series.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Body fat was represented only by BMI (not printed per person); hydration, diet and physical activity, which the authors name as possible sources of variation in release of THC from fat (p. 568, Discussion 2nd paragraph), were not measured.

outcomes.instruments: Immunoassay screen (assay not named; 50 ng/mL cutoff) at three laboratories (LabOne; Navy Drug Screening Laboratory, Jacksonville; Forensic Toxicology Drug Testing Laboratory, Tripler Army Medical Center); GC-MS quantification of THCCOOH after alkaline hydrolysis and liquid-liquid or solid-phase extraction (limit of quantification 2.5 ng/mL); urine creatinine by a modified Jaffe method; THCCOOH normalized to creatinine in ng/mg (p. 563, Specimen collection and analysis).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard forensic laboratory methods; agreement between the three laboratories' screening assays is not reported.
outcomes.operationalization: Positive: immunoassay result of 50 ng/mL or more, not normalized to creatinine; negative: below 50 ng/mL. Time of the first negative and of the last positive specimen in days from admission; days between them (counted as calendar days inclusive, editors' reading of Table II); detection rate: positive specimens in a day divided by all specimens that day, times 100 (p. 563, Statistics).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None reported. Stepwise regression chose among 10 candidate predictors (first-specimen THCCOOH/creatinine, joints a day, days used of the last 14, days since last use, years of use, BMI, sex, age, age at first use, and group) for each of 11 dependent variables, main effects only (p. 563, Statistics).

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive, by group (Table II, pp. 565-566): days to first negative 0.6 (SD 0.8), 3.2 (2.8) and 4.7 (4.8); days to last positive 4.6 (5.6), 9.7 (6.4) and 15.4 (9.8), for the 0-50, 51-150 and above-150 ng/mg groups; ranges 0-16.1 days to first negative and 0-29.8 days to last positive. Regression results are given only as p-values (group with day of first negative p = 0.0021, mean concentration between first negative and last positive p = 0.0202 and day of last positive p = 0.0003; first-specimen THCCOOH/creatinine with the last day with a detection rate of 50% or more p = 0.0001 and days between first negative and last positive p = 0.0002; joints a day with log peak concentration between first negative and last positive p = 0.0383; BMI with day of last positive p = 0.0489) (p. 567, Results 3rd, 5th and 7th paragraphs), without coefficients, intervals or variance explained. The R2 values in Figure 1 (0.9761 to 0.9998) come from straight lines through the three group means (p. 567). The editors' recalculation of each group's means and SDs from the individual rows of Table II reproduces the printed values (last positive of the 0-50 group: 59.2 days over 13 participants = 4.55).
analysis.covariates: Stepwise regression with main effects of the candidate predictors listed above; no adjusted estimates are printed.
analysis.selective_reporting: Days since last use, BMI per person and the regression coefficients are not reported although they were used in the analysis; the text says Table II gives medians and ranges, but the table gives only means and SDs (p. 567, Results 3rd paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Under verified abstinence, screens at the 50 ng/mL cutoff turned negative within a day or two of admission in most of the lowest group but stayed positive for weeks in many of the highest group: 13 of 20 in the highest group were still positive on their last day of observation (mean last day 19, four of them on the 30th day). All times run from admission, not from last use, and the group means of the last-positive times are cut off by the end of observation.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract gives the mean days to first negative and last positive as 0.6 and 4.3, 3.2 and 9.7, and 4.7 and 15.4 without saying that many participants, most in the highest group, were still positive when observation ended, and its 4.3 differs from the 4.6 in Table II and the Discussion (p. 562; pp. 565, 568). The abstract and Conclusions say the data "provide guidelines for interpreting urine cannabinoid test results" and suggest windows for telling new use from residual excretion (pp. 562, 569), but no new use was studied and no rule was tested; the Conclusions' expectation of detection rates of 60-100% for 28 days after the first negative (p. 569) rests on the few participants of the highest group observed that long. The Discussion explains the BMI association by THC stored in fat (pp. 567-568), from a stepwise p of 0.0489 among many uncorrected tests.

timeline.event: Persistence of urinary cannabinoids after supervised abstinence (Dackis et al., 1982), cited by Goodwin among reports of long detection in people who use cannabis frequently (p. 562) and by Moeller et al. (2017) for detection beyond 30 days; not read.
One person took up to 77 days of abstinence to produce 10 consecutive negative specimens at a 20 ng/mL cutoff (Ellis et al., 1985, as cited by Goodwin, p. 562); not read.

Controlled-dosing study proposing a creatinine-normalized ratio between specimens collected at least 24 hours apart to tell new use from residual excretion (Huestis & Cone, 1998, as cited by Goodwin, p. 562); not read.

Narrative review of detection times: THCCOOH detectable for weeks or months in people who use cannabis chronically; in 52 people on a detoxification ward, a mean of 4.9 days and a maximum of 18 days in urine (LOD 10 ng/mL); longest reports 93 and 95 days, called probably exceptional (pp. 202-203)
This study: 60 people under 24-hour surveillance for up to 30 days; last positive screen at 50 ng/mL up to 29.8 days after admission; 13 of 20 in the highest group still positive on their last day.
Same research group: THC found in urine up to 24 days after stopping in a person who used cannabis heavily (Lowe et al., 2009, as cited by Moeller et al., 2017); not read.

Clinical review: urine detection can exceed 30 days after stopping in people who used chronically, and a single exposure in people who do not use cannabis is typically detectable for up to 72 hours (PDF p. 5); Goodwin 2008 is not cited

replication.where_it_stands: Long urinary detection of THCCOOH in people who use cannabis frequently and then stop is reported in the earlier studies Goodwin cites (pp. 562, 567) and in the two reviews read in this batch (Verstraete, 2004; Moeller et al., 2017), which summarize other studies; none of those primary papers was read, so 'partially replicated' rests on these accounts. This study adds verified abstinence and individual data but not times from last use or complete follow-up.

funding.funder: Not stated. No funding, acknowledgment or grant statement is printed; all authors are from NIDA's Intramural Research Program (Chemistry and Drug Metabolism Section) or NIDA's Division of Pharmacotherapies and Medical Consequences of Drug Abuse (p. 562).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: All authors were staff of NIDA (US National Institutes of Health), and the study ran on NIDA's own research unit; presented in part at the 2008 American Academy of Forensic Sciences meeting (p. 562). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A monitored-abstinence study in people whose date and amount of last use are recorded, following everyone until their urine stays negative or analysing time to last positive with survival methods that account for people leaving early, at the cutoffs used in practice (50 and 20 ng/mL screens, 15 ng/mL confirmation), and testing a prespecified rule for telling residual excretion from new use against controlled re-exposure.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Adults who reported regular cannabis use, dependence or abuse and screened positive fit the target (people who use cannabis regularly and are tested), but 77% were men and 83% African American, from one research programme, and recruitment sources are not described.
How participants were recruited, how many were screened and why any were excluded are not reported.

60 participants in groups of 19-21 and 5,916 specimens in Table II are enough to describe the first days, but few remained under observation late: 16 were observed for 27 days or more, and at most 4 of the highest group were observed 24 days or more after their first negative specimen (editors' count).

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Individual demographics and self-reported use are printed (Table I), but the study dates, recruitment, BMI and time since last use are not.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Observation ranged from 0.6 to 30.4 days without reasons for leaving; the last positive time is cut off by the end of observation in 22 of the 54 who ever screened positive (13 of 20 in the highest group), yet group means are presented as detection times; 7 participants gave only 6-8 specimens over 11-12 days; the 6 who never screened positive enter the mean time to first negative but not the mean time to last positive.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods used for identification of the condition
domains.note: Immunoassay screening with GC-MS quantification and creatinine normalization are valid methods, but the immunoassay is not named, three laboratories screened specimens without reported cross-checks, and positive or negative status uses the unnormalized screen.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way for all participants
domains.note: All voids were to be collected and analysed with the same methods, but 7 participants have only 6-8 specimens over 11-12 days (not explained), and one row of Table II (participant F) holds impossible values.

Means and SDs for skewed, cut-off times without survival methods; stepwise regression over 10 candidate predictors and 11 outcomes without correction, reported only as p-values; 'correlations' are lines fitted through three group means.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response rate managed appropriately
domains.note: Numbers approached and screened are not reported, and departures before 30 days are not explained.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist for its descriptive estimates, as the round brief directs for case series. The study's strength is the one that matters most in detection-time research: abstinence was enforced on a closed unit with 24-hour surveillance and random tests, so later positive screens reflect residual excretion, not new use, and every participant's values are printed (Table II). Its weaknesses lie in reporting and analysis: times run from admission, with time since last use unreported; observation ended early for many and the group means of last-positive times are cut off (13 of 20 in the highest group still positive at the end); and there are internal inconsistencies (an impossible row, the abstract's 4.3 against 4.6, 6,158 against 5,916 specimens, the lowest group's 'all negative by eight days' against participant LL, and 2 against 4 participants positive on their last day). The editors summarize the risk of bias as moderate for what the study describes directly. It may be cited for: the setting and sample; each group's and each participant's times to first negative and last positive at the 50 ng/mL screen, read as times from admission and, for the last positive, as minimums; the ranges (0-16 and 0-30 days); 13 of 20 in the highest group still positive on their last day, 4 of them on day 30; 6 of the 16 people observed for 27 days or more still positive at the end; 40% peaking after the first specimen; and the direction of the association with first-specimen concentration. It may not be cited for detection windows counted from last use, for windows at other cutoffs, for the 60-100% daily detection rate at 28 days or the lowest group's 'all negative by eight days' as general rules, for BMI as a cause of longer detection, or as a validated rule for telling new use from residual excretion.

key_findings.finding: Setting and sample: 60 adults (46 men, 14 women; 50 African American; mean age 26.9) who reported cannabis dependence or abuse and smoking a mean of 9.4 joints a week on 10.6 of the last 14 days lived on a closed NIDA research unit under 24-hour medical surveillance with random drug tests for up to 30 days; every void was collected, screened at a 50 ng/mL immunoassay cutoff and quantified by GC-MS.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › Subjects and Specimen collection and analysis; Results, 1st paragraph; Table I (pp. 564-565)

key_findings.finding: Days from admission (not from last use) to the first negative and to the last positive screen, by the THCCOOH/creatinine of the first specimen (mean ± SD): 0-50 ng/mg (n = 19), 0.6 ± 0.8 and 4.6 ± 5.6; 51-150 ng/mg (n = 21), 3.2 ± 2.8 and 9.7 ± 6.4; above 150 ng/mg (n = 20), 4.7 ± 4.8 and 15.4 ± 9.8.
key_findings.locator: Table II, Mean ± SD rows of each group
key_findings.note: The means of last-positive times include participants still positive when observation ended (cut-off values, 13 of 20 in the highest group) and leave out the 6 who never screened positive; the abstract gives 4.3, not 4.6, for the 0-50 group (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Across all participants, the first negative screen came 0 to 16 days after admission and the last positive 0 to 30 days after admission (Table II: 0-16.1 and 0-29.8 days).
key_findings.locator: Table II, columns Time of 1st Negative Specimen and Time of Last Positive Specimen (pp. 565-566); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 568)

key_findings.finding: In the highest group (above 150 ng/mg), 13 of 20 had positive specimens on their last day of observation, which averaged 19 days; for 4 of them that last day was the 30th day of abstinence.
key_findings.note: Editors' count from Table II, counting a last positive on the same calendar day as the end of observation, reproduces 13, a mean of 19.0 days and 4 at 29.7-29.8 days. By the same rule, 4 of 19 in the lowest group (the Discussion says 2) and 5 of 21 in the middle group were positive on their last day: 22 of the 54 participants who ever screened positive.

key_findings.finding: Of the 16 participants observed for 27 days or more, 6, all in the highest group, were still screening positive on their last day (last positive 27.3 to 29.8 days after admission); the other 10 had their last positive between 0 and 20.9 days. Across all groups, 25 of the 54 who ever screened positive had a positive screen 10 or more days after admission; the latest last positives in the lower groups were at 21.8 days (0-50 group, one participant) and 25.3 days (51-150 group).
key_findings.locator: Table II, columns Time of Last Positive Specimen and Length of Observation
key_findings.note: Editors' counts from Table II. Six of the 25 with a positive screen at 10 days or more gave only 6-8 specimens and their last positive equals the end of observation at 11-12 days.

key_findings.finding: Six of the 19 participants in the lowest group (10% of all 60) never screened positive on the unit, and 8 of those 19 had a negative first specimen; two of these 8 screened positive again later (up to 0.7 and 2.2 days after admission).
key_findings.locator: Table II, 0 to 50 ng/mg rows and footnote dagger
key_findings.note: Editors' count. Positive, then negative, then positive again is the pattern the authors describe for the slow terminal elimination phase (p. 562, Introduction 2nd paragraph; p. 567, Discussion 1st paragraph).

key_findings.finding: In 60% of participants the highest creatinine-normalized THCCOOH concentration was in the first specimen; in the other 40% the peak came later, up to 2.9 days after admission.

Mean daily detection rates (share of a day's specimens screening positive) on the day of the first negative specimen were 57.6%, 73.4% and 79.8% in the 0-50, 51-150 and above-150 ng/mg groups. The text and Figure 2 report that in the lowest group all specimens screened negative from about eight days after the first negative, that rates fell more slowly in the middle group, and that in the highest group mean rates stayed between 60% and 100% for 28 days after the first negative.
key_findings.note: The lowest group's eight-day statement conflicts with participant LL in Table II (positive at 21.8 days). The number of participants behind each day of Figure 2 is not shown; from Table II at most 4 of the highest group (T, AAA, SS, Z) were observed 24 days or more after their first negative and only 1 (T) beyond 27 days (editors' count).

key_findings.finding: Between the first negative and the last positive screen, participants gave a mean of 21.1, 47.5 and 91.2 specimens in the three groups, with mean peak THCCOOH/creatinine in that interval of 23.6, 53.4 and 96.4 ng/mg.
key_findings.locator: Table II, Mean ± SD rows (last two columns); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 568)

key_findings.finding: Mean creatinine-normalized THCCOOH fell steeply over the first three days of abstinence in all three groups and then declined slowly over the rest of the stay.
key_findings.note: Daily values in Figure 3 were not extracted.

key_findings.finding: Group and first-specimen THCCOOH/creatinine were associated with the day of the first negative (p = 0.0021), the day of the last positive (p = 0.0003), the last day with a detection rate of 50% or more (p = 0.0001) and the days between first negative and last positive (p = 0.0002); BMI was associated with the day of the last positive (p = 0.0489, higher BMI later) and joints a day with the log peak concentration between first negative and last positive (p = 0.0383). No coefficients or intervals are given.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd, 5th and 7th paragraphs; Discussion, 2nd paragraph (direction of the BMI association)

key_findings.finding: As cited in the introduction, one person in an earlier study needed up to 77 days of abstinence to produce 10 consecutive negative specimens at a 20 ng/mL cutoff (Ellis et al., 1985), and detection time depends on dose, route, hydration, metabolism and excretion, and on assay sensitivity, specificity and accuracy.
key_findings.note: Second-hand; the earlier study was not read.

key_findings.finding: The authors propose that a testing programme normalize a specimen's THCCOOH to creatinine, place it in one of the three groups and read from Table II the expected times to first negative and last positive, the highest expected later concentration and daily detection rates; this rule was not tested against new use in the study.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives 4.3 days as the 0-50 group's mean time to the last positive specimen; Table II and the Discussion give 4.6, and the editors' recalculation from the 13 individual values in Table II is 4.55. Figure 1B's R2 of 0.9998 for the line through the three group means is reproduced with 4.3 (0.99976) but not with 4.6 (0.99897) (editors' calculation), so the abstract and Figure 1B seem to use a different value from the table.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's figure for the lowest group should not be quoted; Table II's value is the one its rows support.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract reports 6,158 urine specimens; the per-participant counts in Table II sum to 5,916 (editors' sum; the group means of that column match the printed means).
reporting_issues.consequence: 242 specimens are unaccounted for in the table; specimens may have been left out of Table II without explanation.

reporting_issues.issue: Table II row F (51-150 group) is impossible: the last positive specimen at 3.1 days comes after observation ended at 2.2 days, and 27 specimens are listed between the first negative and the last positive out of 18 specimens in total.
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one row contains transcription errors, and its values enter the middle group's means.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results and Figure 2 say that in the 0-50 group all specimens screened negative by eight days after the first negative (p. 567), but Table II shows participant LL of that group with a first negative at 0.1 days, a last positive at 21.8 days and 86 specimens in between (p. 565).
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim that people with low initial levels were all negative within about a week is not supported by the study's own table; one of 19 kept screening positive at times for three weeks.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says 2 participants of the 0-50 group had positive specimens on their last day of observation, averaging about 10 days (p. 568); counting as the editors must to reproduce the paper's 13 in the highest group gives 4 in the 0-50 group (A, LL, OO, RR; mean last day 9.0) (Table II).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the number of people in the low group still positive when observation ended is understated.

reporting_issues.issue: Times to the last positive specimen are cut off by the end of observation in 22 of the 54 participants who ever screened positive (13 of 20 in the highest group), but group means and SDs are reported as detection times without survival methods; the 6 participants who never screened positive count as 0.0 days in the mean time to first negative but are left out of the mean time to last positive.
reporting_issues.consequence: The group means of last-positive times are minimums, most of all in the highest group, and the 0-50 group's mean time to first negative (0.6 days) mostly reflects people already negative on arrival.

reporting_issues.issue: Seven participants (FFF, HH, JJ, II, KK, EEE, GGG) gave only 6-8 specimens over 11-12 days of observation, although the methods say all voids were collected (p. 563); six of them never screened negative and their last positive equals the end of observation.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either their urine was collected differently or specimens were left out; their cut-off values raise the means of the two higher groups' last-positive times only to the end of their short stays.

reporting_issues.issue: The 'correlations' between group and outcomes in Figure 1 are straight lines fitted through three group means (R2 0.9761 to 0.9998; how group was coded is not stated); the p-values in the Results come without coefficients; and the text says Table II gives medians and ranges, but it gives only means and SDs.
reporting_issues.consequence: R2 values near 1 say nothing about how well one person's first-specimen concentration predicts that person's detection time; the size of the individual-level associations is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: Participants are described as daily-to-weekly smokers (p. 563), but Table I lists one participant with 0 joints a week and no use in the last 14 days and another with 3 joints a week but no use in the last 14 days; the regression uses joints smoked per day while Table I gives joints per week.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the exposure description is imprecise for some participants.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), J Anal Toxicol 32(8):562-569 (2008), pp. 562-569 (all pages; Tables I-II and Figures 1-3 checked on rendered pages, Table II row F and Figures 1-2 also at 300 dpi; no supplement)
